opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the culture of that place and, honestly, the kind of person Jeremy was. At the time I was really just an undergrad who was excited about robots but didn't have much of a track record. I didn't have papers, I didn't have deep experience in the field. I just reached out and said, essentially, "I'm really interested in this, is there any way I can get involved?"

Looking back, I think what he responded to wasn't my resume — there wasn't much on it — but the enthusiasm and the willingness to just show up and do the work. In robotics especially, so much of the early work is unglamorous: debugging hardware, writing drivers, getting the system to just run at all. A lot of mentors understand that the person who's genuinely curious and persistent is often more valuable than someone with a polished background but less drive.

And I think there's also a generosity there that I didn't fully appreciate at the time. Taking on a student who doesn't know much is a real investment of time and patience. You have to answer basic questions, you have to let them break things. He was willing to make that bet, and it really changed my trajectory. It's the reason I got into research in the first place.

Now that I'm a faculty member myself and I get those emails from students, I think about that a lot. I try to remember that the person on the other end might be exactly where I was — no experience, but a lot of curiosity — and that giving them a chance could matter more than I realize.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Jeremy responded to Xu’s enthusiasm and genuine curiosity about robotics, attributing his willingness to take a chance on him to that passion.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I still think about that a lot, because from his side there was no good reason to say yes. I was an undergrad who cold-called a robotics lab basically out of nowhere. I didn't have a track record in robotics, I didn't have a publication, I had some coursework and a lot of enthusiasm, and that's about it. If I were in his position today, with a lab to run and limited time, I'm not sure I would have picked up that phone and said, "Sure, come in."

So the way I understand it now is partly about him and partly about the moment. On his side, I think Jeremy just had a genuinely low barrier for giving people a shot. He treated it less like hiring and more like, "Let's see what happens if I let this person touch the robot." That's a pretty generous way to operate, and it costs the mentor something, because most of those bets don't pay off. He was willing to eat that cost.

And then on the other side, I think there's something about robotics specifically. It's a field where the gap between knowing the theory and actually making a physical system do anything is huge. So a lot of what matters early on isn't credentials, it's whether you'll keep showing up when the gripper doesn't close and the sensor readings make no sense and you've spent the whole day debugging a cable. He couldn't know that about me from a phone call, but I think he had learned that you only find out by letting someone try.

What that did for me is probably the bigger story. Once you've been on the receiving end of that kind of chance, you feel a sort of obligation to pass it along. So now when a student emails me with no obvious qualifications but a lot of curiosity, I try to remember that I was that email once, and someone decided it was worth the risk.

r001.rationale: The response says Xu had enthusiasm, but explicitly says Fishel could not know from the phone call whether Xu would persist. It attributes the chance to Fishel’s low barrier to giving people a try, not to perceiving Xu’s passion for robotics.

astra-6.text: I think he saw curiosity and a willingness to learn. When I called, I didn’t have much to offer in terms of robotics experience, but I really wanted to get involved. He was willing to give me a chance to see what I could do. Looking back, I really appreciate that. When you’re just starting out, having someone take your interest seriously can make a huge difference.

r001.rationale: The response says Fishel saw curiosity, willingness to learn, and a desire to get involved, but it does not clearly attribute his decision to perceiving Xu’s strong passion for robotics.

sol-6.1.text: I think he saw curiosity and a willingness to learn. When you’re just starting out, you don’t necessarily have much experience to point to, so somebody has to take a chance on your potential. That’s how I understand his willingness to give me an opportunity, and I’m really grateful for it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes Fishel’s decision to Xu’s curiosity, willingness to learn, and potential, but does not say he perceived a strong passion for robotics.
